title: The Power No One Has to Give You
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Drawing on Emmett Murphy's 1996 study of 18,000 managers, which found that people perceived as true leaders value their own competence more than any externally bestowed affirmation, Kathleen Schafer argues that authority and leadership are fundamentally different things, since authority is conferred while leadership is developed by people working to uplift others. Her central distinction is between authority (societally conferred decision-making power) and agency (the ongoing capacity to participate through voice, attention, questions, and refusal), arguing that people who confuse the two mistake themselves for spectators in situations where they are actually participants. She further separates power from control, defining true power as the ability to flow with what is toward what is wanted without needing to force outcomes, and control as inherently precarious because it depends on external conditions like title, alignment, or victory that can always be lost. The piece traces a widely circulated quote from her own earlier work - that leadership is a way of life for those who know who they are, not a matter of men in suits - through its adoption into a project-leadership book chapter and a South African women's leadership program, using its spread as evidence the idea resonates broadly. She closes by reframing the current cultural moment as one confusing position with competence and control with leadership, and argues the corrective is to look within rather than up for the power to change things.
points: Grounds the core claim in Emmett Murphy's empirical study of 18,000 managers across 562 organizations, using its finding - that perceived true leaders value their own competence over external affirmation - as evidence rather than assertion.

Draws a precise operational distinction between authority (conferred, resource- and decision-based) and agency (voice, attention, spending, questioning, refusal), arguing that collapsing the two turns people into spectators in situations where they actually hold participatory power.

Separates power from control by definition: true power is the capacity to move toward a desired outcome without needing to force it, while control is inherently precarious because it depends on maintaining title, alignment, or victory that can always be lost.

Diagnoses a specific cultural confusion - mistaking position for competence and control for leadership - as the reason people look upward for permission to lead rather than recognizing the power already available to them.

Explicitly guards against agency curdling into grandiosity, stating that believing one person can individually solve every problem creates its own dysfunction, and that agency begins with recognizing where one's own participation actually matters.
quotes: Murphy and his associates had studied 18,000 managers across 562 organizations and identified just over 1,000 people who demonstrated exceptional leadership ability. One of the findings was deceptively simple: people perceived as true leaders are those who value their own competence more than any externally bestowed affirmation.
Authority is conferred while leadership is developed and honed by people working to uplift others.
Leadership is not about men in suits. It is a way of life for those who know who they are and are willing to be their best to create the life they want to live.

Authority matters. We give people formal authority because societies and organizations need ways to make decisions, allocate resources, enforce laws, and hold responsibility. But authority is not the same as agency.
Agency is our voice. Our attention. Where we spend our money. What we are willing to question. Whom we invite into a conversation. What we create when what we need does not yet exist.

Control is inherently precarious. If my sense of power depends upon maintaining my title, keeping people aligned with me, accumulating more money, defeating an opponent, or ensuring that others behave as I wish, I am forever at risk of losing it.
This power is impossible for others to take without our consent. And it is what our current moment is asking us to reclaim.
It was never something another person could bestow upon us. It is ours to develop. And ours to choose.
